Digital Brand Communication in the African Economy: A Critical Review of Theory, Practice, and Emerging Issues
venue: British Journal of Mass Communication and Media Research
abstract: With digital technology significantly revolutionizing the way organizations interact with their customers, digital brand communication has become one of the most critical components that can help organizations develop a competitive edge and build long-term relationships with their customers. Even though digital communication has been rapidly developing in the modern world, there is little understanding of digital brand communication in Africa and specifically in Nigeria through the prism of the relevant academic literature. The purpose of this review paper is to analyse the development, theoretical background, drivers, and perspectives of digital brand communication in Africa. Using an approach of narrative integrative review, this paper critically examines existing literature available in various disciplines such as communication, marketing, branding, and information systems in order to gain insight into the concept of digital brand communication in the new digital ecosystem. Some of the key factors that determine effective digital brand communication are social media marketing, personal communication, content marketing, influencer marketing, user generated content, electronic word of mouth, artificial intelligence, omnichannel communication, and mobile first engagement. Digital brand communication is constrained by infrastructural constraints, digital inequality, privacy issues, cyber security threats, regulatory concerns, and cultural diversity. Through the synthesis of Relationship Marketing Theory, Consumer Engagement Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model, a comprehensive theoretical framework for digital brand communication in Africa is proposed by this study. This literature review adds to the body of knowledge through its analysis of digital brand communication in relation to the African context, the development of a comprehensive perspective, and a research agenda that can be used in future research. The results of the study are valuable in their recommendations for the design of ethical and consumer-centric digital branding that could build brand equity and competitive advantage in Africa.

title: Toward safer digital sexual health communication: evaluating the public health reliability of large language model responses on sexually transmitted infections
abstract:
Background 
                     The global burden of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) continues to rise, yet stigma drives many to seek sensitive health information from artificial intelligence chatbots. The quality, safety, readability, and destigmatization of large language model (LLM) responses on sexual health remain under-evaluated, particularly for non-Western models. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     This cross-sectional study constructed 30 standardized English queries (5 themes × 6 questions) informed by Google Trends, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, and patient education platforms, and submitted them to three LLMs—GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Kimi K2.6—via official APIs, in duplicate (180 responses). Two dermatovenereologists (&gt;10 years' experience) rated the responses while blinded to platform identity, across six dimensions (accuracy, completeness, safety, understandability, actionability, and destigmatization) using a five-point scale, supplemented by four readability metrics (FKGL, FRE, GFI, and SMOG). Primary analysis used linear mixed-effects models retaining all individual ratings; the original aggregated non-parametric pipeline was retained as a sensitivity analysis. title: Framing Insecurity in North-West Nigeria: A Conceptual Analysis of Social Media Actors and Nigeria Police Force Narratives
venue: Azman University International Journal of Management and Social Sciences
abstract: The proliferation of social media has transformed the communication ecology of insecurity in North-West Nigeria by enabling citizens, journalists, security agencies, and non-state actors to compete in framing conflicts. While the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) seeks to frame insecurity through official narratives emphasizing operational successes, public reassurance, and institutional legitimacy, social media actors frequently construct alternative frames highlighting government failure, human suffering, insecurity, and distrust in state institutions. This conceptual paper examines the competing frames employed by social media actors and the Nigeria Police in communicating insecurity across Northern Nigeria. Guided by Framing Theory, the study adopts a conceptual research design based on documentary analysis of scholarly publications, government reports, media studies, and policy documents. The paper argues that framing contests between institutional and citizen-generated narratives significantly shape public perceptions of insecurity, confidence in security institutions, and national discourse on conflict management. The study concludes that while social media democratizes security communication by amplifying marginalized voices, it also accelerates misinformation, emotional polarization, and competing truth claims. Conversely, official police communication often prioritizes institutional legitimacy over transparency, thereby widening public distrust. The paper recommends adopting evidence-based strategic communication, collaborative digital engagement, and transparent crisis communication to enhance public confidence and strengthen democratic policing in Nigeria.

title: Empowerment or exploitation? reconsidering women's social media entrepreneurship in the gig economy
abstract: Social media has fundamentally transformed contemporary entrepreneurial practices. Social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Pinterest and YouTube have allowed people to set up businesses that require minimal startup capital and a quick reach to people around the world. Social media has significantly influenced women's entrepreneurial participation in the economy, creative selfemployment and flexible working opportunities, with the propensity to increasingly engage in these activities through digital platforms (Ghosh et al., 2022).However, more recently, the creation of what is called the creator economy and platform mediated entrepreneurship has further shifted social media from a promotional tool to an entrepreneurial infrastructure that now impacts on the visibility of creators, their engagement with audiences, monetisation of their content, and how the entrepreneurs' commercial sustainability is shaped (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;van Dijck et al., 2018). Although these developments have brought new possibilities for women entrepreneurs to sell their products in markets and develop sustainable digital ventures, they have also exacerbated the reliance on market platforms and algorithmic visibility, as well as on ongoing communicative labour. Today, entrepreneurial success increasingly depends on entrepreneurs' ability to navigate platform rules, cultivate audience relationships, and adapt strategically to evolving platform ecosystems.Social media has significantly expanded entrepreneurial opportunities for women by lowering barriers to market entry, reducing start-up costs, and facilitating direct access to geographically dispersed consumers (Ghosh et al., 2022). These affordances have enabled women to establish creative enterprises, cultivate entrepreneurial identities, and participate more actively in digital economies. At the same time, entrepreneurial success increasingly depends not only on business capability but also on sustained platform visibility, audience engagement, and algorithmically mediated communication. Communication therefore becomes more than a promotional activity; it constitutes a productive form of entrepreneurial labour through which visibility, legitimacy, and commercial sustainability are continuously negotiated within platform ecosystems.The developments are a sign of the fact that social media entrepreneurship is more than a technology or an economic phenomenon. Instead, platform governance, communicative work, and algorithmic visibility are now more and more vital aspects of entrepreneurial achievement. Thus, a conceptual model is needed that is able to reflect both entrepreneurial opportunity and platform dependency in the entrepreneurial experience of women.The aim of the opinion paper is to rethink social media entrepreneurship of women, looking at it from the lens of platform capitalism, digital labour, feminist media studies and communication studies. Instead of entrepreneurship being merely a means for empowerment, this paper suggests that the success of the entrepreneur depends more and more on communicative labour, emotional branding and algorithmic visibility. Building upon recent discussions of platform-dependent entrepreneurship (Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024), this paper proposes the Platform-Dependent Woman Entrepreneur as a communication-centred conceptual framework that extends existing theory by foregrounding the gendered communicative, emotional, and algorithmically mediated dimensions of entrepreneurial dependence within platform economies.There are a few studies that have contributed to our knowledge of digital entrepreneurs, platform workers, influencers and content creators, but none has addressed the full range of these roles. However, as a social media entrepreneur, a woman holds a unique position in platform economies as she is not only a business owner but is also structurally dependent on privately-controlled digital platforms for demonstrating her entrepreneurial visibility, reaching audiences and achieving commercial viability. While working in platform business markets, women entrepreneurs have to negotiate algorithmic visibility, communicative expectations, and emotional performances as well as business management, in contrast to conventional entrepreneurs who are mainly impacted by their competitive capability. Feminist scholarship also indicates that women's experiences of platform participation are often distinct from men's due to the expectation that women are more authentic, emotional, responsive, aesthetic and vulnerable to online gendered hostility when visible as entrepreneurs. Hence, platform dependency should be seen not only as a dependency on technological aspects, but also as a dependency on gendered communicative expectations that give rise to opportunities and constraints for the entrepreneur. Entrepreneurship in social media is fundamentally different from traditional business entrepreneurial activity since entrepreneurial value is not just from the production and exchange of goods and services, it is generated from a continuous communicative interaction with platform ecosystems. Entrepreneurs should be aware of visibility, audience engagement, platform insights, and continuously evolve their communication approach for algorithmic-driven spaces. Thus, communicative, relational and affective activities become fundamental parts of entrepreneurial activity, instead of marketing. As such, from a digital labour perspective entrepreneurial communication is a productive labour which creates value for both the entrepreneur and the digital platforms (Gajjala, 2018;Terranova, 2000). Women's social media entrepreneurship, therefore, should not be considered only as an activity of participating in the market but also as a participation in the platforms-based labour system, whose success is increasingly based on the need for ongoing communicative performance.In digital economies, the distinction between productive labour, self-expression, identity performance and leisure have gotten increasingly blurred, as digital labour itself has long maintained (Terranova, 2000). Women entrepreneurs are a great example of this shift as entrepreneurial success is becoming more and more dependent on their ability to create content, engage in social media, tell a story, and build their own brand as an internet personality as well as a business owner. These communicative practices create economic value for both the entrepreneur and the platform owners, the audience and the advertisers, thus, perpetuating the quasidependence of the entrepreneur on the algorithms and systems of visibility that run through the platform (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;van Dijck et al., 2018).In addition to productive labour, women entrepreneurs engage in a lot of affective and relational labour by interacting with their audience, managing their community, being emotionally responsive to their audience and building trust with their audience. Feminist scholarship has long established that these kinds of labour are expected mainly of women since entrepreneurial success is often seen as being related to authenticity and emotional accessibility, not just entrepreneurial competence (Gill, 2007;Hochschild, 2012). While they are largely hidden in traditional entrepreneurship studies, these communication practices are essential for economic value because they help to keep audiences loyal, keep people on the platform and help to preserve entrepreneurial continuity.The feminisation of communicative labour is particularly evident in the realm of creator cultures, where technology has led to the development of para-social relationships, where women entrepreneurs must be constantly in touch with followers, must share a part of their life and must demonstrate emotional authenticity in becoming a successful entrepreneur. Such labour goes far beyond simply the promotion; it's an investment that creates the visibility, trust, engagement and value of platforms all at once. Communication then serves more than just as a facilitator of entrepreneurial activity, it is also economically productive labour that is engaged in the reproduction of entrepreneurial identities and commercial sustainability.Digital labour therefore provides an important explanation for how entrepreneurial value is produced within platform economies. However, understanding women's entrepreneurship requires moving beyond digital labour alone to examine how algorithmic governance, platform dependency, and communicative expectations jointly shape entrepreneurial opportunities and constraints.Today, being platform-dependent has become a major characteristic of social media entrepreneurship. Social media entrepreneurs rely on entrepreneurial visibility, audience reach, and commercial sustainability, unlike traditional businesses which compete mostly in terms of their products, services, or positioning in the market, and rely on private and self-governing digital infrastructures that regulate their visibility, audience, and sustainability. Platform algorithms not only influence entrepreneurship opportunities but also the entrepreneurial strategic capabilities of the entrepreneurs themselves, as they determine what is visible, discoverable and thus economically worthwhile in the platforms (Bucher, 2018;Gillespie, 2019).Entrepreneurial success is therefore increasingly tied to the ability of entrepreneurs to constantly adjust to the changing recommendations systems, platform policies and algorithmic governance.There is a basic paradox associated with platform dependency. Digital platforms significantly lower the cost of entry into entrepreneurship, as they offer low-cost access to markets and audiences, as well as to digital infrastructures. Meanwhile, they concentrate visibility, monetisation, and the access of audiences into their own closed and algorithm-driven systems, which they keep mostly hidden from entrepreneurs. For entrepreneurs, the outcome of their business can change drastically due to changes in their algorithmic recommendations, content moderation or even monetisation policies, without anything changing in their entrepreneurial ability or product quality (Cotter, 2019;B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023). But entrepreneurial risk is now more and more governed via platform control mechanisms as opposed to just market competition. Entrepreneurial sustainability is thus more than an enhancement of entrepreneurial competence, and relies on the ability to negotiate ongoing algorithmic uncertainty, as the entrepreneur's job.Although platform dependency explains entrepreneurs' structural reliance upon digital infrastructures, entrepreneurial success is ultimately realised through communication. Visibility, legitimacy, and commercial sustainability emerge through communicative practices that continually translate algorithmic exposure into audience relationships and economic value.In platform economies, the function of communication is not only to promote but to become a productive entrepreneurial practice as well. In addition to creating products or providing services, entrepreneurs have to constantly tell stories about themselves, new audiences, remain visible, and create a continuity of communication on platforms. Algorithmic visibility thus makes communication an economically productive endeavour as the success of entrepreneurs more and more hinges on the ability to keep the audience engaged with a content rather than just one-off promotions (Abidin, 2020;Gillespie, 2019).Communicative labour can be defined as the ongoing creation of content, emotional interaction with audiences, responsiveness to the interaction on the platforms, and the performance of entrepreneurial authenticity. These communicative expectations are not gender-neutral and can be seen when comparing the experiences of men and women in the context of feminist media scholarship. Compared to their male counterparts, women entrepreneurs are more likely to be expected to look approachable, to be at the touch of the audience, to be authentic and appear at all times to be emotionally available and good looking (Gajjala, 2018;Gill, 2007;Marlow & Mcadam, 2013). Thus, entrepreneurial communication is both a means of economic production and gendered labour, it produces entrepreneurial visibility and it is not visible as labour.By treating communication as labour, communication scholarship expands to not just focus on the role of communication as a medium for facilitating entrepreneurial learning and leadership, but one where entrepreneurial identities, economic opportunities, and platform visibility are being continually produced.Communicative labour explains how entrepreneurial visibility is produced, whereas emotional branding explains how that visibility is sustained through continuous identity performance and audience engagement.Emotional branding has turned into the vital part of the platform-based entrepreneurship. Unlike traditional companies, social media business owners are increasingly developing a personal identity for themselves, their daily life, emotions and lifestories into entrepreneurial communication to build credibility, trust and maintain relationships with audiences. In the context of creator economies, visibility is not the only way of being entrepreneurial, because the continuous selfdisclosure and relational communication of the creator is also a key entrepreneurial resource (Abidin, 2020;Jane, 2016).However, the communicating expectations at the same time increase emotional pressure on entrepreneurs. Women entrepreneurs have become more and more expected to be 'always on', emotionally attuned, genuine and personally available, whilst at the same time being expected to oversee the performance of the business. These pressures are not due to the fault of individual entrepreneurs; rather, they are a consequence of the nature of the platforms and their algorithms that encourage constant interaction, responsiveness and visibility. Research literature on platform labour is increasingly showing that these are structural conditions of platform labour and control, rather than indicative of individual failures to cope. (Bucher, 2018;Gajjala, 2018;Gillespie, 2019).The developments mirror other cultures of entrepreneurial self-optimisation, where being visible is an ongoing entrepreneurial duty, not just a promotional task.Algorithmic relevance is a key driver of entrepreneurial success and is a process that requires constant content creation, engagement and identity performance. Thus, emotional branding must be seen less as a marketing strategy but as an integral part of communicative labour in which entrepreneurs manage their sustainability on a constant basis in platform economies.The increasing "always-on" entrepreneurialism is noteworthy for the involvement of women, as entrepreneurial work is now part of the performance of identity.Women entrepreneurs are expected to sell products and services, and do it through authenticity, positivity, being emotionally resilient and accessible. Consequently, emotional branding should not be understood solely as a marketing strategy but as an integral component of platform labour. Entrepreneurial success increasingly depends upon the continuous performance of authenticity, emotional accessibility, and relational engagement, reinforcing the interdependence between communication, entrepreneurial identity, and platform capitalism.Women's social media entrepreneurship is often discussed in the narratives of empowerment, independence, flexibility as well as financial inclusion. Digital platforms have clearly increased business opportunities by reducing start-up costs, and providing more flexibility on how to work, and by offering a new avenue for generating income for women who are facing barriers in traditional labour markets (Ghosh et al., 2022;Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024). This progress has enabled numerous women to create innovative businesses, cultivate a sense of entrepreneurship and be more engaged in digital economies.But the opportunities should not be romanticised as an example of unqualified entrepreneurial empowerment. The very same infrastructures of platforms are also those that control visibility, monetisation, audience reach and commercial sustainability by proprietary algorithmic systems as well. Therefore, the structural dependence cannot be completely overcome by entrepreneurial ownership because ongoing communicative work, emotional brand, algorithmic responsiveness and interaction with the audience have become the basis for success in commercial ventures.The theme of empowerment can then be said to have the effect of individualizing entrepreneurial success and to mask the underlying structure that generates entrepreneurial opportunities. Entrepreneurs have limited control over platform governance and algorithmic inequality, non-paid communicative labour, emotional exhaustion, and visibility dependence. As such, the failures of entrepreneurs can then be understood as personal failures that result from larger platforms infrastructures which control economic participation.Moreover, platform entrepreneurship is often not institutionalized in the same way as traditional work with benefits like income security, labour rights, and health insurance, and support measures from the organizations. Women who become entrepreneurs in creator economies in turn then find themselves in a situation of entrepreneurial autonomy and economic precarity, typical symptoms of platform capitalism (Vallas & Schor, 2020;Wood et al., 2019). Gendered forms of online harassment, cyberbullying, reputational attacks and constant visibility anxiety experienced by women as entrepreneurs and creators in platform environments (B. E. Duffy & Meisner, 2023;Jane, 2016) further amplify these structural vulnerabilities.These structural conditions suggest that the experiences of women entrepreneurs cannot be adequately understood through narratives of empowerment alone.Although digital platforms undoubtedly expand entrepreneurial opportunities, they also embed entrepreneurs within communication systems governed by algorithmic visibility, platform policies, and continuous audience engagement. Entrepreneurial success, therefore, increasingly depends upon communicative labour, emotional performance, and sustained platform participation rather than solely upon entrepreneurial capability or innovation. Understanding these intersecting dynamics requires a conceptual framework that recognises both the opportunities created by digital platforms and the structural dependencies they simultaneously produce. This dichotomy of empowerment and exploitation is therefore, not enough to explain women entrepreneurship in the social media. At the same time, the digital platforms open up entrepreneurial opportunities and place entrepreneurs in the network of algorithmic governance, communicative labour, emotional branding and platform dependency. Women's experiences as entrepreneurs are thus not fully empowered nor entirely exploited but rather are ongoing struggles for entrepreneurial freedom and platform dependency. It is necessary to have a conceptual framework that can incorporate both aspects of the dynamics, instead of focusing on just one aspect.Recent scholarship has made significant contributions to our understanding of entrepreneurship in a digital context, including the notions of digital entrepreneurship, platform work, creator labour and platform-dependent entrepreneurship. Digital entrepreneurship is a research field that investigates how digital technologies enable entrepreneurs to develop and generate value for ventures (Nambisan, 2017), creator labour research studies the nature of labour relations, algorithmic governance of platforms (Wood et al., 2019), and visibility labour, content production and audience engagement (Abidin, 2020;B. Duffy & Wissinger, 2017). More recently, platform-dependent entrepreneurship was conceptualised to explain entrepreneurs' increasing reliance on platform infrastructures (Yu & Sekiguchi, 2024). While these views offer valuable insights, they fail to capture the gendered communicative and emotional aspects of platform dependency of women social media entrepreneurs.The present paper does not attempt to say that women constitute a completely distinct category of entrepreneurs. But, it proposes that when entrepreneurial activity is situated in the context of gendered expectations of visibility, authenticity, emotional accessibility and relational engagement, it takes on a different communicative texture and form than platform dependency. The proposed framework is an extension of platform dependency theory, and explicitly includes these gendered communicative processes in the conceptualisation of entrepreneurial dependence. The framework is grounded in the surrounding legacy of research and theory, such as those of creator labour, platform work, influencer research, and emotional labour. These literatures explore various empirical populations but have a shared interest in entrepreneurial activity that relies on the continual communication, audience engagement, algorithmic visibility and emotional performance of platform infrastructures. These literatures, therefore, are used as informative analogues from a theoretical perspective and not as solid empirical data for women entrepreneurs. Empirical future studies are needed on the dynamics of the various types of digital entrepreneurship by women. Communication scholarship needs to shift away from "heroic" projections of digital entrepreneurship and explore the political economy of platform-mediated work critically.First, future studies are needed to examine the impacts of algorithms on the visibility of entrepreneurs and economic inequality. Platform infrastructures have a significant impact on the visibility, engagement and monetisation opportunities that are made available to entrepreneurs.Second, the emotional and psychological implications of the 24/7 digital presence of women entrepreneurs need to be studied. Burnout, anxiety, self-surveillance and emotional exhaustion are becoming more and more central experiences in platform economies.Thirdly, intersectionality needs to be further highlighted in the field of social media entrepreneurship. Platform labour experiences are linked to class, race, geography, language and access to digital technologies, shaping who can participate, gain visibility, and sustain entrepreneurial success within platform-based economies.Communication research, therefore, needs to acknowledge the inequalities in opportunities and vulnerabilities in digital entrepreneurial cultures.Lastly, the study of platform governance and platform labour regulation should be critically addressed by communication scholars. Discourses for entrepreneurship in the present tend to focus on the individual's strength and self-optimisation without holding structural accountability for digital capitalism. Such efforts would contribute to more equitable platform governance and more inclusive digital entrepreneurial ecosystems for women entrepreneurs.Social media entrepreneurship is one of the most salient expressions of today's digital work. Platforms are crucial for women entrepreneurs in terms of economic involvement, creativity and as a space to be more visible as entrepreneurs. These opportunities are, however, parallel to those of precarious job opportunities that are common in the gig economy and platform capitalism. title: Beyond static responses: multi-agent LLM systems as a new paradigm for social science research
abstract: Abstract As large language models (LLMs) transition from static tools to fully agentic systems, their potential for transforming social science research is well recognized. This paper introduces a structured framework for understanding the diverse applications of agentic LLM systems, ranging from simple data processors to complex, multi-agent systems capable of simulating emergent social dynamics. By mapping this developmental continuum across six levels, the paper clarifies the technical and methodological boundaries between different agentic architectures, surveying current capabilities and future potential. It highlights how lower-tier systems streamline conventional tasks like text classification and data annotation, while higher-tier systems enable new forms of inquiry, including the study of group dynamics, norm formation, and large-scale social processes. However, these advancements also raise challenges around reproducibility, ethical oversight, and emergent biases. The paper critically examines these concerns, arguing for sound validation methods, interdisciplinary collaboration, and standardized evaluation metrics. It argues that while agentic LLM systems offer considerable potential for the social sciences, using them responsibly will require careful, context-sensitive deployment and ongoing methodological refinement. The paper concludes with a call for future research that balances technical innovation with ethical responsibility, working toward agentic systems that not only replicate but also extend social science methodology.

title: DIGITAL STORYTELLING AS A STRATEGIC TOOL FOR COUNTERING MISINFORMATION, HATE SPEECH, AND CONFLICT ESCALATION ONLINE
venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive
abstract: Digital communication has transformed how societies produce, circulate, and interpret information, creating opportunities for participation while accelerating misinformation, hate speech, polarization, and conflict escalation. This study examines the potential of digital storytelling as a strategic communication intervention for countering harmful online narratives and strengthening conflict prevention. The study adopts an integrative analytical approach that synthesizes scholarship on digital storytelling, misinformation, narrative persuasion, strategic communication, and peacebuilding to examine the mechanisms through which storytelling may influence conflict-related attitudes and behaviours. The analysis traces how harmful narratives are produced, amplified, and interpreted through identity and emotion, and evaluates digital storytelling interventions across narrative credibility, corrective capacity, humanization, audience engagement, trusted-messenger influence, and conflict-sensitive dissemination. Particular attention is given to whether these mechanisms can reduce misinformation susceptibility and hostile stereotypes while strengthening empathy, dialogue, intergroup trust, counter-speech, information resilience, and social cohesion. The analysis also considers platform dynamics, community participation, digital literacy, algorithmic amplification, ethical risks, and unintended consequences that may condition intervention effectiveness. By linking these analytical dimensions across narrative, behavioural, community, and peacebuilding outcomes, the study assesses the conditions under which digital storytelling demonstrates potential to disrupt pathways from harmful online narratives to polarization and conflict escalation. The resulting integrated framework positions digital storytelling not as a substitute for fact-checking, moderation, or offline peacebuilding, but as a complementary strategy for strengthening information resilience and expanding credible, nonviolent alternatives within polarized digital environments.

title: Political Communication Dysfunction: The Impact of Controversial Statements by Public Officials on Public Trust
venue: Journal of Legal Political and Humanistic Inquiry
abstract: The increasing prevalence of controversial statements by Indonesian public officials during the 2024–2025 period has generated public criticism and raised concerns regarding declining trust in government institutions. This study aims to analyze the relationship between political communication dysfunction and public trust erosion by examining the characteristics of controversial statements, digital media amplification mechanisms, and their implications for democratic governance. This research employs a qualitative normative library research approach based on documentary analysis of official statements, government documents, public trust reports, academic literature, and credible media sources. The analysis integrates Political Communication Theory, the OECD Framework on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions, Aristotle’s Rhetorical Theory, Castells’ Communication Power Theory, and Coombs’ Situational Crisis Communication Theory. The findings reveal that controversial statements represent systemic communication dysfunction rather than isolated individual failures, affecting public trust dimensions, particularly integrity, responsiveness, and fairness. Digital media accelerates the spread of negative narratives through agenda-setting, framing, and echo chamber mechanisms, while ineffective crisis responses further weaken institutional credibility. The study concludes that strengthening communication accountability, digital literacy, empathetic leadership, and institutional crisis communication mechanisms is essential for restoring public trust and supporting democratic governance in Indonesia’s digital era.

title: Countering climate misinformation with large language models: Evidence from ChatGPT
abstract: Public support for climate action hinges on the integrity of information environments. In an online experiment, U.S. adults used ChatGPT to evaluate climate-related claims. We first conducted computational text analysis of GPT conversation logs, assessing valence, formality, bias, recency, authority cues, and semantic richness of ChatGPT’s responses using language-model based classifiers and link-level metadata. Concurrently, we measured credibility judgments for both the claims and ChatGPT’s responses through participant self-reports. Credibility perceptions were driven primarily by individual differences; greater acceptance of the scientific consensus, attention to climate change, prior familiarity with ChatGPT, and younger age predicted higher perceived credibility. Once these factors were accounted for, authority cues were associated with slightly less extreme climate attitudes, while positive valence and semantic richness correlated positively with perceived credibility. These results support transparent, unbiased, audience-tailored engagement as a pathway to strengthen responsible climate communication and help bridge the gap between scientific consensus and public understanding.

title: Assessing and Countering Health Misinformation on Social Media to Safeguard Public Trust in Medicine
venue: European Journal of Prosthodontics and Restorative Dentistry
abstract: The spread of health misinformation through social media platforms has transformed into a serious sociomedical threat in undermining public trust on medicine, health professional’s scientific institutions and public health authorities. This manuscript looks into how health-related false or misleading narratives spread on Facebook, Twitter/X, TikTok, YouTube, WhatsApp, and other similar platforms, especially during public health emergencies like the COVID-19 outbreak. Health misinformation has the potential to change one’s risk perceptions, lessening acceptance of vaccination, promoting unsafe treatments, delaying appropriate care-seeking, and reducing adherence to evidence-based recommendations. According to the review, cognitive mechanism refers to the propagation of rumors as misinformation spreaders are often incapable of disarming popular claims with evident truth. This paper also describes specific monitoring approaches, including social listening, text mining and natural language processing, coding frameworks, and citizenscience validation. It will require coordinated action by healthcare professionals, public health institutions, governments, researchers, media organizations and social media platforms. Strategies include open communication about risks, rapid correction of false claims, promotion of credible sources, digital health literacy, ethical content moderation, platform accountability, and community-based engagement. To maintain public confidence in medicine, it is essential to not only correct misinformation but also enhance the credibility, accessibility and responsiveness of health communication systems.

title: Artificial intelligence and infodemic management: a governance framework for digital public health decision-making
abstract: Background Digital communication ecosystems have profoundly transformed the circulation of health information. During public health crises, large volumes of information—including misinformation and disinformation—can spread rapidly across online platforms, generating complex information environments commonly described as infodemics. These dynamics can influence public risk perception, undermine trust in health institutions, and affect adherence to preventive measures. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies have created new opportunities for monitoring information flows and identifying emerging misinformation patterns in real time. However, the translation of AI-generated insights into coordinated public health decision-making processes remains limited. Methods This study developed a conceptual governance framework aimed at explaining how AI-generated insights derived from digital information ecosystems can be translated into evidence-informed public health responses. The framework was developed through a secondary conceptual analysis of the complete evidence extraction database generated from a previously published scoping review including 63 studies. The methodological approach combined thematic synthesis of empirical evidence with conceptual modeling techniques commonly used in public health systems research. Results The synthesis of the literature identified several thematic domains describing how digital technologies and artificial intelligence are used to monitor and respond to health misinformation within digital communication ecosystems. Building on these domains, this study proposes a governance-oriented conceptual framework integrating digital data ecosystems, artificial intelligence analytics, interpretive public health expertise, and institutional governance mechanisms. Conclusions Artificial intelligence technologies offer powerful tools for monitoring complex digital information environments, yet their integration into public health decision-making requires governance models capable of linking analytical insights with institutional responses. The proposed framework contributes to the emerging field of digital public health governance by providing a structured conceptual model for translating AI-generated insights into coordinated public health actions during infodemic events. Although the framework remains preliminary and requires formal validation, it provides a structured conceptual basis for future empirical implementation and governance research.

title: Developing a Deep Learning-Based Artificial Intelligence System for Detecting Scientific Misinformation on Digital Platforms
venue: Middle East Journal of Communication Studies
abstract:
Objectives: This study develops and evaluates an Arabic scientific misinformation detection system by fine-tuning AraBERT-base-v2. It examines the effects of early stopping and input sequence length on model performance, interprets selected linguistic characteristics associated with misleading content, and discusses the limitations of using machine-translated data.
Methodology: The study adopted a mixed-methods design, employing a systematic integration of quantitative and qualitative approaches, supported by an interpretive qualitative reading. The initial database consisted of 23,546 records, including 123 Arabic articles collected from the Akeed, Sheek, and Taqeen platforms, and 23,423 foreign-language records drawn from the GossipCop and PolitiFact collections within FakeNewsNet. After data cleaning, 73 Arabic articles were retained for descriptive and interpretive analysis, while the foreign-language data were machine-translated into Arabic using the MarianMT model (Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-ar), and subsequently cleaned and linguistically normalized. The final dataset used in the model experiments comprised 21,595 records, divided into 17,276 records for training and 4,319 records for validation. The binary classification into genuine and misleading content was based on the sources' original labels. Fine-tuning of the AraBERT-base-v2 model was then carried out through three experiments: the baseline model, early stopping, and an increased sequence length of up to 512 tokens.
Results: The findings revealed that the baseline model achieved the highest classification accuracy (80.9%) in detecting scientific news; however, it exhibited signs of overfitting. In contrast, applying the Early Stopping strategy improved the balance between performance and stability, achieving an accuracy of 75.7% while enhancing the model's generalization capability. Increasing the maximum sequence length to 512 tokens resulted in a lower accuracy (73.1%), likely due to the inclusion of irrelevant information. Furthermore, the model demonstrated superior performance in identifying fake scientific news compared with genuine scientific news.
Conclusion: The findings indicate that AraBERT is an effective tool for classifying Arabic scientific misinformation. However, achieving optimal performance requires a careful balance between data quality and the training strategies employed. The results also emphasize the importance of regularization techniques, such as Early Stopping, in mitigating overfitting and improving model generalization, whereas increasing the input sequence length does not necessarily lead to better performance. Accordingly, the study recommends prioritizing improvements in dataset quality and diversity, together with careful hyper parameters tuning, to support the development of more efficient and reliable misinformation detection systems for real-world applications.

title: Holocaust education in networked publics: audience responses to a facebook campaign against holocaust distortion
abstract: Abstract This study examines audience responses to “Proteggi I Fatti”, an Italian Facebook campaign developed within the European project Deconstruct: Deconstructing and Countering Holocaust Distortion via Campaign , Education and Training . The campaign aimed to raise awareness of Holocaust distortion and denial by disseminating historically accurate information and supporting critical engagement with online content. The analysis is based on 10,160 public comments collected from the comment sections of nine Facebook posts published between December 2024 and May 2025. Methodologically, the study combines lexical and bigram analysis, sentiment analysis, word embeddings, and LLM-assisted classification through the Gemini API, followed by manual validation. Findings show that many users reframed the campaign’s educational messages through the lens of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, especially the war in Gaza. Recurring patterns include Holocaust distortion, Nazi analogies, victim-perpetrator reversal, and accusations that Holocaust memory is instrumentalized for political purposes. The paper contributes to research on digital Holocaust education by showing how social media campaigns may become sites where remembrance, political conflict, antisemitism, and distortion intersect. It also highlights the value and limits of AI-assisted methods for identifying implicit and context-dependent forms of Holocaust distortion in platformed publics.

title: Media Literacy in the Age of Misinformation: Challenges and Responsibilities of Journalism Education
abstract: Abstract The rapid transformation of the media environment from traditional mass media to digitally networked communication has fundamentally altered the ways in which information is produced, distributed, consumed, and interpreted. The expansion of social media, mobile communication, algorithmically curated platforms, user-generated content, and generative artificial intelligence has created unprecedented opportunities for access to information while simultaneously increasing exposure to misinformation, disinformation, manipulated content, and other forms of information disorder. In this environment, Media and Information Literacy (MIL) has emerged as an essential competency for citizens and, more particularly, for journalism students who are expected to become professional gatekeepers, interpreters, verifiers, and disseminators of information. This article examines the significance of media and information literacy in the age of misinformation and critically analyses the challenges and responsibilities of journalism education in developing competent, ethical, and verification-oriented journalists. The study adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and conceptual approach based on a critical review of scholarly literature, institutional frameworks, research reports, and contemporary developments in journalism and digital media. Particular attention is given to the historical evolution of media literacy, the changing information ecosystem, misinformation and disinformation, verification practices, fact-checking, algorithmic influence, digital technologies, and the emerging implications of generative artificial intelligence for journalism education. The study draws upon Media Literacy Theory, Gatekeeping Theory, and Social Responsibility Theory to develop an integrated theoretical framework. The analysis indicates that journalism education can no longer be restricted to conventional reporting, writing, editing, and production skills. It must incorporate critical thinking, source evaluation, digital and visual verification, fact-checking, data and algorithmic literacy, ethical reasoning, and responsible use of artificial intelligence. The study argues that media literacy should be repositioned as a core professional competency within journalism education rather than being treated as an optional or peripheral skill. Strengthening media literacy among future journalists can contribute to professional credibility, public trust, democratic participation, and the integrity of the wider information ecosystem.

title: A Human-centered Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence and a Single Pulmonologist’s Responses in Pulmonary Medicine Communication
venue: The Anatolian Journal of General Medical Research
abstract: Objective: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients and the public to access medical information.In pulmonary medicine, where information needs span a wide range of chronic and potentially serious diseases, the quality of artificial intelligence-generated communication requires systematic evaluation. Methods:This cross-sectional comparative study evaluated responses to 37 standardized pulmonary medicine questions covering major respiratory domains.Each question was answered by four LLMs-Gemini 2.5, GPT-4, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek v3.2-and a board-certified professor of pulmonology with more than 25 years of clinical experience.Six blinded raters, including three pulmonologists and three laypersons, assessed anonymized responses using a five-point Likert scale across conceptually aligned domains: accuracy/perceived reliability, clarity, and scientific adequacy/practical usefulness.Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).Comparative analyses were performed using repeated-measures one way analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons and Friedman tests.Results: Inter-rater reliability indicated slight single-measure agreement (ICC 0.09-0.12)and fair-to-moderate average-measure agreement (ICC 0.36-0.45),which is consistent with the subjective nature of communication-focused assessment.Overall, LLM-generated responses received higher communicationquality ratings than physician-generated responses across evaluation domains.Gemini 2.5 and GPT-4 achieved the most favorable scores, particularly on accuracy/perceived reliability and clarity.Differences between LLMs and the physician were more pronounced among lay raters than among expert raters.Among expert raters, physician-generated responses were rated among the highest for accuracy and scientific adequacy, although this pattern was not observed for clarity.Conclusion: Contemporary LLMs may provide clear, reliable, and practically useful information on pulmonary medicine, particularly as perceived by lay users, when evaluated from both expert and lay perspectives.These findings support their adjunctive use in patient education and health communication and emphasize that LLMs cannot replace clinical judgment, professional accountability, or physician oversight.

title: Social Media and Political Communication in India: Transforming Electoral Politics, Public Discourse, and Democratic Engagement
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has fundamentally transformed political communication in India, reshaping interactions among political actors, citizens, journalists, and institutions. The proliferation of affordable smartphones, declining mobile data costs, and widespread adoption of social media platforms have enabled political parties to communicate directly with voters, mobilize supporters, and influence public discourse on an unprecedented scale. Simultaneously, these developments have altered the relationship between traditional and digital media, giving rise to a hybrid communication environment in which political narratives circulate across multiple interconnected platforms. This paper examines the evolving role of social media in India's political communication ecosystem by synthesizing contemporary scholarship on electoral campaigning, citizen participation, agenda setting, digital mobilization, misinformation, and democratic deliberation. Rather than viewing social media as either inherently democratizing or inherently detrimental to democracy, the paper argues that digital platforms constitute a contested political arena whose democratic consequences depend upon institutional contexts, patterns of platform use, and existing social inequalities. While social media has expanded opportunities for political participation, increased accessibility to political information, and enabled new forms of citizen engagement, it has also intensified challenges relating to misinformation, online polarization, digital exclusion, and the weakening of traditional journalistic gatekeeping. The paper concludes that understanding political communication in contemporary India requires moving beyond technologically deterministic explanations towards a contextual approach that recognizes the interaction between digital platforms, political institutions, media organizations, and India's complex socio-political landscape.

title: Advancing theory in social media-mediated crisis communication research in China: A mixed-method review
More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
abstract: This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.

title: Early Post-Publication Behavioural Signals of Misinformation on Social Media
abstract: Social-media users often encounter contested claims before professional fact checks become available. This study examines whether the expression of seed posts and the early audience responses they receive differ across nine Snopes claim-level verdict categories, and whether these behavioural signals support prospective classification. The corpus links 588 public X seed posts to 28,600 quote-post observations during the first 24 hours. Analyses preserved the associated Snopes article as the grouping unit and assessed the temporal onset of distributional differences, the contribution of textual, affective, and engagement features, and predictive performance at prespecified early cutoffs. Among posts with observed quote activity, six of nine verdict categories met the one-vs-rest persistence criterion from hour 1, and 33 of 36 class pairs met the criterion at some point during the first day. Category-associated differences in post expression and audience response therefore became observable early at the group level. Individual classification, however, remained modest and non-monotonic. The strongest hour-1 macro- was .237, compared with .113 for the strongest dummy baseline, and performance did not improve systematically through hour 24. Seed-post features carried substantial early information, while quote-content and engagement features added more limited information as responses accumulated. Early post-publication behaviour provides a temporally resolved account of how posts associated with different claim-level verdicts are expressed and received, but it does not permit reliable stand-alone prediction of the associated claim-level verdict. The study provides a behavioural benchmark for future research on human–platform interaction and carefully evaluated decision support.

title: The Influence of Social Media Platforms on the Spread of Political Propaganda and Misinformation in Nigeria's 2023 Presidential Election; Implications for Future Elections
abstract: The 2023 Nigerian presidential election witnessed unprecedented use of social media platforms as vehicles for political propaganda and misinformation.This study investigates how platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Whats-App influenced the dissemination of biased narratives and deceptive content during the election period.The problem centres on understanding the extent to which social media shaped voter perceptions and potentially impacted electoral integrity.The objective is to explore the mechanisms of propaganda spread, identify patterns of misinformation, and assess implications for future electoral processes in Nigeria.Using a qualitative methodology, this research relies on content analysis of social media posts, newspapers reports and internet materials.This approach facilitates an in-depth understanding of how misinformation circulates and affects public opinion during critical political events.The study adopts the Agenda-Setting Theory as a theoretical framework, which explains how media influences public priorities by highlighting specific issues, thereby shaping perception and behaviour among audiences.Key findings reveal: (1) social media platforms served as primary channels for rapid dissemination of politically motivated misinformation; (2) coordinated campaigns by partisan actors exploited algorithmic biases to amplify divisive and false content; (3) many voters lacked sufficient media literacy to critically evaluate the authenticity of online information, increasing vulnerability to propaganda.Recommendations include:(1) strengthening digital literacy programs nationwide to empower voters in discerning credible information online; (2) enhancing regulatory frameworks to obligate social media companies to monitor and curb the spread of harmful misinformation; (3) fostering collaboration between electoral bodies, civil society, and technology firms to deploy real-time fact-checking and public awareness campaigns during elections.

title: Application of Computer-Simulation-Based Clinical Case Training for General Practice Clinical Reasoning in Standardized Residency Training: A Digital Health Communication Perspective
abstract: Clinical reasoning is a core competency in standardized residency training for general practitioners, yet conventional case-based instruction is often constrained by limited clinical exposure, inconsistent case complexity, and insufficient opportunities for repeated decision-making practice. This study explores the application of computer-simulation-based clinical case training to improve clinical reasoning among general practice residents from a digital health communication perspective. A digital simulation environment was designed to present interactive clinical cases integrating patient history, symptoms, examination findings, laboratory results, and dynamic clinical feedback. Residents were required to collect information, identify clinical problems, formulate differential diagnoses, select appropriate examinations, and develop management plans through sequential decision-making processes. The digital platform also supported real-time feedback, standardized communication pathways, and repeated case-based learning, enabling trainees to review their reasoning processes and identify decision-making errors. The effectiveness of the training approach was evaluated by comparing clinical reasoning performance, diagnostic accuracy, decision-making efficiency, and learner engagement before and after the intervention. The findings indicate that computer-simulation-based clinical case training can provide a structured, interactive, and repeatable learning environment that supports the development of diagnostic and clinical decision-making abilities. From the perspective of digital health communication, the approach also facilitates more effective information exchange, feedback delivery, and interaction between learners and simulated clinical scenarios. This study suggests that computer-simulation-based training may serve as a valuable supplementary strategy for enhancing clinical reasoning and digital competency in standardized general practice residency training.

title: A MULTI-MODAL DEEP LEARNING AND DATA MINING FRAMEWORK FOR EARLY DETECTION OF MISINFORMATION IN SOCIAL MEDIA NETWORKS
venue: International Journal of Progressive Research in Engineering Management and Science
abstract: Social media platforms have been instrumental in transforming communication and sharing information in the digital world.These social media platforms are not only helping people disseminate information but are equally responsible for the dissemination of misinformation, fake news, manipulated media, and propaganda.Today, the spread of misinformation has become a global issue that poses a threat to public health, economy, political decisions, and the general well-being of people around the globe.Conventional approaches for the detection of misinformation are based on traditional machine learning algorithms.They use handcrafted features and classifiers which are incapable of analyzing multi-modal data that is being used in misinformation these days.In this paper, we propose a novel Multi-Modal Deep Learning and Data Mining Framework for the early detection of misinformation in social media networks.Our framework will make use of NLP, CNN for image analysis, and GNN for graph-based analysis.Moreover, data mining techniques will also be used to discover patterns and anomalies.We will evaluate our framework through experiments based on benchmark datasets for misinformation detection.Moreover, the results show that graph-based spreading patterns and visual content analysis play an important role in the early detection of misinformation prior to its viral spread.This proposed methodology contributes towards intelligent misinformation analytics, trustworthy AI-powered content moderation, and robust digital information systems.

title: Algorithmic curation and deliberative democracy: A critical analysis of echo chambers, platform governance, and digital public discourse
abstract: Scholarship on social media and deliberative democracy has converged on a single, repeated claim since roughly 2015: that social media both enables and undermines democratic discourse. This claim no longer advances the field, because it does not specify which architectural feature of a platform produces which deliberative outcome, and because it rarely tests its own assumptions against direct evidence of platform governance decisions. This study isolates algorithmic curation, as distinct from social media as a communication medium, as the primary object of analysis, and asks what effect it has on deliberative democracy, why that effect occurs, and how it can be governed. The study conducts a qualitative thematic synthesis of fifty-two English-language secondary sources, drawn from an initial pool of eighty-three records identified through structured searches of Google Scholar, JSTOR, SSRN, and Scopus-indexed journals, screened against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, and coded against four deliberative norms: inclusiveness, reasoned argumentation, reciprocity, and reflexivity. The coded literature is read against four documented cases of platform governance: Meta’s January 2025 termination of third-party fact-checking, the measured limits of X’s Community Notes system, the structural fragility of Mastodon’s federated moderation model, and Nepal’s September 2025 Gen Z movement, in which a government ban on twenty-six platforms triggered mass protest and a subsequent selection of an interim prime minister conducted partly through a hundred-thousand-member Discord server. Social media expands the formal opportunity to participate while algorithmic amplification reproduces existing inequalities of voice; engagement-optimized ranking, not social media as a medium, is the mechanism most responsible for the decline of reasoned and reciprocal exchange; and current institutional responses, crowd-sourced correction, federated decentralization, and crisis-driven hybrid deliberation, each restore some deliberative capacity but none restores it fully. Deliberative democratic theory needs a distinct, empirically grounded account of algorithmic governance, built on a broader evidentiary base than the Western regulatory literature it has so far relied on.

title: Beyond the 5G-COVID moment: the scope of EMF mis- and disinformation on German-language social media
abstract: Public perception of health risks from electromagnetic fields (EMF) and 5G mobile networks diverges persistently from the scientific evidence base, a gap increasingly shaped by social media. While existing research has examined the acute COVID-5G conspiracy episode on individual platforms, systematic multi-platform analyses of the broader EMF misinformation landscape remain scarce. This study presents a mixed-methods analysis of EMF and 5G-related misinformation across YouTube, Telegram, and Twitter/X in German-language social media, combining automated classification, sentiment analysis, and topic modelling with structured qualitative content analysis. The three corpora comprise over 430,000 posts from more than 16,000 accounts, covering content published primarily between 2019 and 2024. The analysis reveals that EMF misinformation circulates in a predominantly pseudo-expert communicative register rather than overtly inflammatory language, is structurally embedded within broader conspiracy ecosystems rather than circulating as standalone content, and is sustained by commercial incentive structures alongside ideological motivations. The three platforms serve complementary functional roles within an integrated distribution network. While the pandemic-era peak in activity has subsided, the underlying network infrastructure remains intact. The findings establish an empirical baseline for the German-language EMF misinformation landscape against which future developments, including the impact of generative AI on misinformation production, can be measured.

title: ‘Can you see empathy?’ exploring social media posts as a performance of organisational empathy
Digital Distrust: Patient-Centred Communication and the Calibration of Epistemic Reliance in the Era of Online Self-Diagnosis and AI Symptom Checkers
venue: Journal of Medical Clinical Case Reports
abstract: Background: Patients are coming to consultations informed by search engines, social media and generative AI. Clinicians may characterize this as distrust of clinicians. Actualities are messier, and our language for talking about how communication breaks down is limited. Purpose: Operationalize the concept of digital distrust, disambiguate it from related concepts with which it is often confused, and report a communication framework grounded in theory for clinical practice. Methods: Methodology is an interpretive conceptual integration, described per guidelines for conceptual articles and interpretive description. We performed an iterative, theory-driven integration of peer-reviewed scholarly literature from digital health, health communication, judgement and decision-making, and bioethics scholarship, interpreted by the first author’s practice-grounded understanding developed across over thirty years of clinical nursing practice. No primary data were generated or analyzed. Findings: Five themes emerged from our analysis. Pre-informed consultations are normalized. Conversational fluency is becoming dissociated from clinical credibility. Checking behavior is varied depending on information source, with conversational artificial intelligence (AI) less often double-checked than search engines. Rather than merely possessing divergent epistemic authorities, patients navigate them. Patients also hold back information to preserve the relationship. The interpersonal exchange is where trust is appraised or misappraised. Implications: We reconceptualize patients' digital distrust as an epistemic recalibration gone awry at the margins of an otherwise benign revolution in information access, rather than a generalized loss of faith in clinicians. We propose five working categories of digitally mediated stance that patients take during consultations, as well as the Digital Calibration Protocol (DCP), a four-step communication maneuver (Acknowledge – Clarify – Educate – Reframe). Conclusion: Blanket acceptance or rejection of patients' digital content is indefensible. Patient-centered communication provides a mechanism for recalibrating patients' reliance. Here, we introduce the DCP as a hypothesis-generating framework in need of empirical testing.

title: Beyond Keywords: Comparing LLM-Assisted Topic Modeling Approaches Across Political Communication Contexts
Political memes and influence in the Global South: Calibrated prediction of misinformation and opinion change
venue: Online Journal of Communication and Media Technologies
abstract: Memes have become a routine infrastructure of political talk across platforms, blending humor, affect, and compressed commentary. Yet scholarship often alternates between strong causal claims and descriptive accounts, leaving open what can be predicted—reliably and with well-calibrated probabilities—from lightweight survey signals. We compare an interpretable penalized logistic regression (ridge) and a flexible random forest to model three self-reported outcomes among Salvadoran university students (cross-sectional survey; n ≈ 162): perceived misinformation potential of memes, perceived manipulation potential, and self-reported opinion change after viewing memes. Predictors were derived from closed and multiple-selection items capturing (a) most-used platforms (TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and X), (b) common emotions when seeing memes (laughter, reflection, annoyance, and indifference), (c) verification practice (yes/no), and (d) confidence in meme messages (ordinal 0-2). Two operational indicators captured multiple selection (multi_platform and multi_emotion). Models were evaluated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation; classification thresholds were selected on training folds only. We report discrimination (AUC-ROC), threshold-dependent metrics (balanced accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity), probabilistic accuracy (Brier score), and decile-based calibration. Predictive performance was highest for perceived misinformation (AUC-ROC ≈ 0.85-0.86; Brier ≈ 0.10), moderate for perceived manipulation (AUC-ROC ≈ 0.74-0.75; Brier ≈ 0.17), and lowest for opinion change (AUC-ROC ≈ 0.70-0.74; Brier ≈ 0.21-0.23). Across models, multi_platform selection and confidence emerged as recurrent signals. Findings are presented as predictive rather than causal and motivate richer measures of exposure and context to model opinion change.

title: Technology Is Global, Accountability Is Not: Platform Asymmetry, AI Disinformation and Linguistic Justice in Asia
venue: Journal of Arts Humanities and Linguistics
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming the global information environment by reshaping how information is produced, distributed and verified. While debates on AI governance have largely focused on technological innovation, regulation and geopolitical competition, less attention has been paid to how protection against AI-generated disinformation is distributed across linguistic communities. This article argues that a central inequality of the AI era lies not only in unequal access to digital technologies but also in the uneven distribution of platform accountability and verification capacity.Drawing on scholarship on platform governance, surveillance capitalism, digital colonialism and journalism studies, the article develops the concept of platform asymmetry to explain how global technology platforms allocate moderation resources, safety infrastructures and accountability mechanisms unevenly across linguistic communities. It also introduces the concept of the asymmetry of verification, referring to the widening gap between the democratization of synthetic content production and the unequal distribution of resources required to authenticate information.Using qualitative comparative case studies of Myanmar, India and Indonesia, alongside policy analysis and insights from multilingual journalistic practice, the article examines how linguistic inequalities in platform governance affect journalism’s democratic role. It argues that AI-generated disinformation should be understood not only as a technological challenge but also as a challenge of information justice, because unequal platform protections create unequal conditions for verification and public knowledge production.The article proposes language equity as a normative principle for AI governance. It argues that digital justice requires a more equitable distribution of multilingual moderation systems, verification infrastructures and accountability mechanisms. Unless accountability becomes as global as the technologies themselves, artificial intelligence risks reinforcing existing inequalities within the global information order and weakening journalism’s capacity to sustain informed democratic communication.
